\section{OpenGM: preserving the question across optimization and inference}
\label{sec:exec24-opengm-reuse}

A bank allocating a servicing budget may need the least costly joint action,
the probability that a particular account responds, or the effect of changing
the assignment policy. These are different questions even when their data
can be represented by the same factor graph. OpenGM is a useful historical
reference for separating model representation, algebra and algorithms. Its
generality makes the adapter's declaration of the requested operation more
important, not less. A most probable joint configuration is not a vector of
marginal probabilities, and neither is automatically a causal intervention
\cite{exec24_opengm_paper,exec24_opengm_source,exec24_opengm_choice}.

\subsection{A historical original with a conditional integration route}
The selected repository is \texttt{opengm/opengm}, pinned to its 26 July
2019 revision. Its README explicitly labels the project unmaintained, while
the inspected CMake file declares version 2.3.1. The README links manuals
for other versions; those labels must not be silently treated as the
selected artifact. This is a bounded historical-source comparison, not a
claim that every later fork or commercial support arrangement has been
surveyed. The five-page 2012 library paper is a genuine retained original.
Its design argument is inspected directly, while its historical performance
comparisons are not imported as current measurements
\cite{exec24_opengm_paper,exec24_opengm_source}.

The root license grants MIT-style permissions with notice retention. That
does not determine the complete rights of a binary containing optional
solvers. CMake exposes separate switches for, among others, CPLEX, Gurobi,
libDAI, graph-cut libraries, HDF5 and Python bindings. The inspected defaults
disable the command-line build and Python wrapper. A list of supported
interfaces therefore does not establish what an installed artifact contains.
The selected source's build requirements and declarations are evidence for
a proposed artifact inventory; no downloaded code or build script has been
executed \cite{exec24_opengm_source}.

The proposal retains OpenGM as a reference and leaves a narrowly specified
isolated worker as a conditional integration option. Direct adoption of the
whole solver catalogue is deferred because its algorithms have different
domains, rights and result contracts. Porting is deferred until a measured
need justifies maintaining model encodings, numeric behavior and solver
interfaces. The unmaintained declaration increases the importance of an
identified maintenance owner and a supported build, but is not by itself a
proof that every bounded use is unsuitable \cite{exec24_opengm_choice}.

\subsection{The algebra is part of the business query}
Let $V$ be finite variables, $F$ factors, $x$ a joint labeling, and
$\phi_f(x_{N(f)})$ a factor on its ordered neighborhood. OpenGM separates
the operation that combines factors from the operation that accumulates
over labelings. For a probability model, an unnormalized weight is
\[
 w(x)=\prod_{f\in F}\phi_f(x_{N(f)}),\qquad
 Z=\sum_x w(x),\qquad p(x)=w(x)/Z,
\]
provided the factors give finite nonnegative weights and $0<Z<\infty$.
For an energy model, $E(x)=\sum_f e_f(x_{N(f)})$ may instead be minimized.
The library paper formalizes these as different algebraic choices. It also
explicitly warns that not every algorithm supports every choice. Selected
source implements separate addition, multiplication, minimization and
maximization operations. A type name or successful generic serialization
cannot replace the algorithm-specific compatibility check
\cite{exec24_opengm_paper,exec24_opengm_source}.

An exact authored example makes the distinction operational. Suppose two
binary labels have joint probabilities
\[
 p(0,0)=0.35,\quad p(0,1)=0.25,\quad p(1,0)=0,\quad p(1,1)=0.40.
\]
The most probable joint labeling is $(1,1)$, but $P(X=0)=0.60$. Under
unit loss for an incorrect prediction of $X$, choosing its marginal mode
has expected loss $0.40$, whereas taking the $X$ component of the joint
mode has loss $0.60$. For 10,000 hypothetical cases at 100 USD per error,
that substitution adds 200,000 USD expected loss. The solver could have
correctly solved its stated joint optimization problem while the business
adapter answered the wrong question \cite{exec24_opengm_choice}.

Even correct probability inference does not identify an intervention.
Let an unobserved fair binary $U$ determine $Y=U$, and let the assigned
action equal $U$ with probability $4/5$. Then $P(Y=1\mid A=1)=4/5$, while
both intervention means are $1/2$ and the effect of changing $A$ is zero.
Conditioning a factor graph on $A=1$ preserves the selection association;
it does not remove the assignment mechanism. A causal worker needs an
identified model and a declared mechanism transformation before numerical
inference is meaningful \cite{exec24_opengm_choice}.

\subsection{A normal return does not certify exhaustive search}
The selected brute-force routine enumerates configurations with variable
zero changing fastest. It updates an incumbent through the chosen ordered
accumulator, invokes a visitor, and stops if the visitor requests it. Both
visitor stopping and exhaustion reach a final \texttt{NORMAL} return.
The separate visitor protocol distinguishes, for example, a time-limit stop
from a bound-based stop, but that distinction is not preserved in this
routine's return code. Its \texttt{arg} method supports the first stored
labeling and returns \texttt{UNKNOWN} for a requested higher rank. These
are concrete source contracts, not a report from an installed worker
\cite{exec24_opengm_source}.

For a two-variable authored energy table, let the enumeration order
$(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ have energies $5,4,3,0$. Stopping after two
visits produces incumbent $4$; complete enumeration produces $0$.
The four-unit difference is known because this tiny example has an exact
oracle. In a larger case, \texttt{NORMAL} alone does not supply either an
exhaustion certificate or a finite optimality gap. The proposed response
must therefore include the visited/requested state counts where meaningful,
visitor stop reason, incumbent, independently valid bound and algorithm
configuration \cite{exec24_opengm_choice}.

The inherited base inference interface further returns an inverse-neutral
value for its default bound when the accumulator has an ordering, and a
not-a-number value when it does not. For floating-point minimization,
the selected inverse neutral is negative infinity. The brute-force class
does not override that bound in the inspected header. Exhaustion may justify
an exact result under valid arithmetic, but merely reading its default bound
does not yield a useful finite certificate. Unsupported marginals return
\texttt{UNKNOWN} in the base interface. A uniform response schema must
preserve those distinctions instead of manufacturing a probability or gap
\cite{exec24_opengm_source}.

\subsection{Hard constraints and shared factors require numerical contracts}
A second boundary appears in the concrete move-making delegate. For a
multiplicative model it recomputes the destination objective. For other
operators it updates the previous value by combining a new factor value
and removing the old one. With finite exact arithmetic this is a useful
incremental calculation. With infinite penalties it can have a different
numeric contract \cite{exec24_opengm_source}.

Consider an additive unary energy whose initial label has positive infinite
penalty and whose other label has zero penalty. The exact constrained
optimum is the feasible second label. Along the inspected incremental
update, the arithmetic expression is $+\infty+0-(+\infty)$, which is
not-a-number under the independently tested binary64 arithmetic. This is a
conditional source witness: no native OpenGM failure was observed, and
other algorithms or encodings may follow different paths. It motivates
fixtures for initially infeasible states, infinite penalties, NaNs and
finite substitutes. Replacing infinity by an arbitrary large constant is
not automatically valid; the constant must dominate a proved objective
range without creating unacceptable numeric error
\cite{exec24_opengm_source,exec24_opengm_choice}.

Function sharing saves representation space but does not remove repeated
factors. An authored unary factor with weights $(2,1)$ gives probability
$2/3$ to its first label after normalization. Adding the same factor twice
multiplies its contribution twice and yields $4/5$, a change of $2/15$.
That may be the intended model, or it may double-count one observation.
The adapter must distinguish shared storage identity from independent
evidence provenance \cite{exec24_opengm_paper,exec24_opengm_choice}.

Variable order is another semantic input. The inspected factor constructor
requires strictly increasing variable indices using runtime checks that
remain active when ordinary debug assertions are disabled. Other label
checks are assertions, and one direct-evaluation label check is commented
out in the selected source. This does not prove every invalid call lacks
validation; it requires entrypoint-specific tests. Sorting variable indices
must also permute factor axes. For a binary table with weights
$w(0,0)=1,w(0,1)=2,w(1,0)=3,w(1,1)=4$, the correct $P(X=1)$ is $7/10$.
Transposing its semantic axes changes the reported event probability to
$3/5$. Both tables normalize, so a sum-to-one check cannot detect the
meaning change \cite{exec24_opengm_source,exec24_opengm_choice}.

The proposed qualification suite starts with tiny fully enumerated models,
where energy optima, partition functions and marginal probabilities have
separate exact oracles. It varies semiring, solver, factor and variable
order, shared function identity, numeric type, constraint encoding and
early visitor stops. It tests valid inputs and typed refusals separately.
Even 40 binary variables have $2^{40}=1{,}099{,}511{,}627{,}776$ joint
assignments; finite representability is not a practical exhaustive-search
guarantee. Sparse or shared functions can reduce storage while leaving
the search combinatorics difficult \cite{exec24_opengm_choice}.

An isolated CLI or MCP worker should declare its exact artifact, enabled
solver dependencies, model algebra, supported factor class and requested
result. Its output distinguishes model rejection, unsupported algorithm,
timeout, incomplete incumbent, numeric failure and qualified result. A
timeout must preserve request identity and partial-result status; a retry
must not duplicate a business action. These are proposed adapter contracts,
not verified OpenGM integrations \cite{exec24_opengm_choice}.

Scientific ownership covers causal meaning and loss; numerical ownership
covers algebra, domain and valid bounds; adapter ownership covers ordering,
termination and request recovery; platform ownership covers maintenance,
rights and complete cost. A hypothetical 18,000 USD over 600 submitted,
450 completed and 300 qualified requests gives 30, 40 and 60 USD per request
under the respective denominators. Actual current support, compatibility,
prices and decision value remain unknown. Public tests can resolve bounded
implementation questions before expensive bank experiments. Hidden
assignment, unrestricted causal identification and arbitrary uncertainty
cannot be supplied by a general factor-graph solver. Package execution and
independent validation remain to be performed
\cite{exec24_opengm_choice}.

The chapter's comparisons locate several different causes of an apparently
successful but unusable answer. A bridge can change variable meaning, a
predictor can answer a conditional rather than interventional question, and
an inference engine can solve the wrong numerical objective. Even the right
objective may have unsupported probability terms or an inadequate numerical
approximation. The shared service must preserve the question at each of
these steps. The authoritative software choice in
Chapter~\ref{scisyn:software} therefore remains selective reuse with explicit
scientific and numerical boundaries; these examples explain the obligations
behind that choice.

\chapter{Functional discovery, symbolic identification and estimating equations}
\label{v13:sw-functional}

\section{An operation is defined by its mathematical output}

A bank may ask a single software team to discover a graph, identify an effect
and estimate the value of an offer. Those requests have different outputs.
Discovery can return a selected directed graph, an equivalence class or a set
of candidates. Identification can return an expression in the observed law or
a nonidentification result. Estimation can return a number with a sampling
uncertainty claim. A shared product becomes misleading when it places all
three behind a field named ``causal effect'' without preserving these types.

Consider a renewal offer $A$, retained balance $Y$ and customer characteristics
$X$ available before the offer. A point-treatment question might be
\[
 \theta=\mathbb E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\}.
\]
Here the expectation is over a declared eligible population, not automatically
over the customers who accepted an offer. A discovery algorithm can help
propose relationships among $X,A,Y$, but a graph proposal does not by itself
establish that $Y(a)$ is identified. Even after identification, numerical
uncertainty depends on how customers were sampled and whether branch, household
or calendar dependence matters. Software comparison must preserve each stage.

The selected source paths considered here make these differences concrete.
DirectLiNGAM exposes a functional discovery construction; y0 exposes symbolic
identification; delicatessen exposes estimating equations; and statsmodels
exposes fitted treatment-effect operations with a joint GMM representation.
These are useful components of a workflow, with different scientific contracts.
The source inspections establish the specific interfaces and branches described
below. They do not establish execution speed, numerical agreement or empirical
coverage for this bank. \cite{v13_sw_lingam,v13_sw_y0,v13_sw_delicatessen,v13_sw_statsmodels}

\section{DirectLiNGAM: a selected order and the meaning of prior knowledge}

The inspected DirectLiNGAM class accepts a prior-knowledge matrix, an option to
apply it softly, a measure named \texttt{pwling}, \texttt{kernel} or
\texttt{pwling\_fast}, and a choice about adaptive-Lasso pruning. Its fit method
checks the prior matrix shape, selects variables sequentially, residualizes
remaining variables, stores a causal order and calls a separate adjacency
estimation routine. The fast branch refers to an additional GPU implementation;
the inspected dispatch is not a performance measurement. \cite{v13_sw_lingam}

The motivating functional family can be written
\[
 X_j=\sum_{k\in\operatorname{pa}(j)}b_{jk}X_k+\varepsilon_j,
\]
with an acyclic order and assumptions on the disturbances that distinguish this
family from unrestricted latent-confounded systems. A selected order narrows the
model much more than a CPDAG. That narrowing can be appropriate when its
functional assumptions are defensible; it cannot be justified by comparing only
the number of directed edges with a constraint-based method that deliberately
retains ambiguity. The present interface inspection does not verify the base
adjacency estimator or provide a finite confidence statement for the selected
order.

Prior knowledge is particularly consequential. The source describes zero as no
directed path, one as a directed path, and minus one as unspecified knowledge.
A bank statement that ``offer acceptance occurs after invitation'' is a temporal
constraint. It is not necessarily a statement that a directed path must exist.
Likewise, a field absent from the available dataset is not a justified absent
cause. An adapter should retain the original proposition, its variable order,
its path-versus-edge meaning and the evidence supporting it. Transposing an
array or treating an unknown entry as zero can change the scientific problem
without causing a matrix-shape error.

For funding analysis, useful adverse cases include a latent common market shock,
near-Gaussian disturbances and aggregation that mixes several decision times.
A comparison should ask whether the supplied functional model is valid in each
case, what output the package produces when it is not, and whether downstream
reporting preserves that limitation. It should not credit a plausible-looking
order as proof of an identified funding response. Constraint-based CPDAG/PAG
methods, alternative functional models and additional experimental information
are substantive alternatives, each requiring its own declared assumptions.

The appropriate first reuse candidate is an adapter around a reviewed operation.
Chapter~\ref{v131:graph-uncertainty} develops the base-class orientation and
total-effect calculation that this dispatch alone does not establish. A port
still needs matched behavioral references, dependency terms and a maintenance
case. The observed MIT license is evidence for that investigation, not a
completed dependency or maintenance assessment. \cite{v13_sw_lingam}

\section{y0: an expression can fail to exist before estimation begins}

The inspected \texttt{identify\_outcomes} function accepts an acyclic directed
mixed graph, treatment and outcome variables, optional conditions and an optional
ordering. With no conditions it dispatches to an ID routine; otherwise it
dispatches to IDC. It catches a dedicated \texttt{Unidentifiable} exception,
returning \texttt{None} by default and re-raising when \texttt{strict=True}.
This is a useful explicit boundary between a symbolic expression and a failure
to identify the requested query. It is only the dispatcher. The detailed
comparison in Section~\ref{exec18:pyid-packages} excludes the selected native
conditional path pending a separation repair, while the following chapter
traces recursion and graph validation. Recognizing this entry point cannot
override those narrower findings or establish general correctness. \cite{v13_sw_y0}

For example, suppose the graph justifies adjustment for pre-offer $X$. The
corresponding functional, under the relevant causal assumptions, is
\[
 \theta=\int\{m_1(x)-m_0(x)\}\,dP_X(x),
 \qquad m_a(x)=\mathbb E(Y\mid A=a,X=x).
\]
The expression states what must be estimated. It supplies neither fitted
regressions nor a sampling distribution. If instead the graph contains an
unblocked latent common cause of $A$ and $Y$ and no identifying information,
another optimizer cannot manufacture this adjustment functional.

A product therefore needs separate outcomes for an identified expression, a
scientifically nonidentified query, an unsupported query language and an
execution error. Mapping all of them to a numeric missing value loses essential
information. Conversely, turning \texttt{None} into zero would state that the
effect is zero, which is a different scientific claim. The adapter should bind
the graph, query, conditioning variables and expression identities, and retain
the original failure type and diagnostic context.

Counterfactual coverage also needs care. The existence of an ID/IDC entry point
does not establish support for every nested counterfactual, path-specific effect
or transport query. The proper comparison has a query matrix: adjustment,
general intervention identification, conditional interventions and other
counterfactual families. Each cell should be tied to an inspected algorithm and
an independent small-graph reference. Package branding is not evidence for every
cell. A proposed symbolic adapter is justified as a candidate by this source;
general algorithmic correctness and comprehensive query support remain open.

\section{Stacked equations preserve the nuisance contribution}

Delicatessen's inspected \texttt{ee\_aipw} function returns an array of estimating
equations rather than a fitted effect object. Its parameter vector contains the
effect, two potential-outcome means and propensity/outcome coefficients. The
documentation and source identify a $(3+b+c)\times n$ array, where $b$ and $c$
are the numbers of propensity and outcome coefficients. The source selects
logistic or linear outcome regression from the outcome values unless the user
forces a continuous treatment of the outcome. It clips estimated propensity
probabilities only when bounds are supplied. \cite{v13_sw_delicatessen}

Writing $e(x)=P(A=1\mid X=x)$ and $m_a(x)=\mathbb E(Y\mid A=a,X=x)$, the
familiar augmented mean contribution has the form
\[
 \phi_a(O)=m_a(X)+\frac{\mathbf 1\{A=a\}}{p_a(X)}
                   \{Y-m_a(X)\},
 \qquad p_1=e,\quad p_0=1-e.
\]
This display describes the target contribution; its causal interpretation still
requires consistency, exchangeability and positivity for the declared target.
Stacking nuisance equations alongside equations for the two means makes their
joint role explicit. To obtain an estimator one must solve the system; to obtain
uncertainty one must review its Jacobian, covariance construction and sampling
unit. An array of equations is not an already qualified sandwich estimator.

This distinction matters when borrowers are clustered. If $\psi_i(\eta)$ is
an estimating-function contribution, an independent-customer covariance uses
individual outer products. A group construction instead uses sums
$\Psi_g(\eta)=\sum_{i\in g}\psi_i(\eta)$ and outer products of those group
sums, under an appropriate group sampling law. Neither replacing a variable
name nor using a generic robust standard error proves the required result for
shared calendars or persistent audit errors. The solver and covariance paths
must be inspected and qualified separately.

Truncation is also part of the method. Replacing $\widehat e$ by
$\max(\epsilon,\min(1-\epsilon,\widehat e))$ controls numerical weights but
changes the estimating equation. For a bank with almost no offers in a risk
stratum, clipping cannot create the missing counterfactual support. An adapter
must record the requested and applied bounds, how many observations were
affected, and the sensitivity of the answer. A stable answer after clipping is
not evidence that positivity held before clipping.

The same module exposes instrumental-variable and two-stage least-squares
estimating-equation entries. Their presence identifies a useful review route;
it does not establish weak-instrument inference, longitudinal g-estimation or
arbitrary dependent-data support. Reusing a selected equation as an independent
numerical reference may be valuable even when a complete estimator is not yet
an adoption candidate. \cite{v13_sw_delicatessen}

\section{statsmodels: population and covariance must survive the interface}

The inspected \texttt{TreatmentEffect} class describes five methods: IPW,
regression adjustment, AIPW, AIPW with weighted least squares and IPW with
regression adjustment. It states that inference uses a joint GMM representation
of the selection model, outcome model and effect functions. Its current outcome
model is documented as linear OLS. The result class exposes contrasts for an
effect and two potential-outcome means. \cite{v13_sw_statsmodels}

The population option distinguishes all, treated and untreated observations.
These correspond to different questions. With treatment propensity $e(X)$,
the all-population target averages over $P_X$, whereas an effect among treated
customers averages over $P_{X\mid A=1}$. Matching point estimates across packages
requires matching this measure as well as the outcome and treatment coding.
An apparent disagreement can be a population mismatch rather than a numerical
defect; apparent agreement in one synthetic sample can conceal the mismatch.

The class also exposes \texttt{ps\_bounds}, defaulting to $(0.001,0.999)$, and
validates strictly interior, ordered bounds. The selected source says the same
bounds apply to point estimates and GMM moment conditions. That is part of a
reproducible comparison, including a comparison with delicatessen's optional
truncation. Omitting these settings from a bridge specification means the two
programs need not be solving the same estimating equations.

One especially important detail is the internal \texttt{\_cov\_type} argument.
The inspected class states that it affects preliminary estimators but that final
GMM results correspond to HC0. A caller cannot infer clustered or calendar-robust
final inference merely from passing a covariance-related keyword. The early
module header also contains older prose about unavailable standard errors,
while the class and result implementation contain joint-GMM inference. Reviewing
the current operation resolves more than searching for one favorable or
unfavorable sentence. \cite{v13_sw_statsmodels}

For a banking baseline, this makes the candidate scope concrete: a declared
point-treatment population, linear outcome model, explicit propensity bounds
and a reviewed sampling law. Panel or time-series capabilities elsewhere in
statsmodels require separate inspection; they are not established by this one
module. The correct reuse decision is provisional numerical integration and
matched equation review, with refusal of unsupported dependence claims.

\section{A matched comparison must keep the question fixed}

A useful comparison first fixes the eligible population, intervention, observed
history and identification assumptions. It then asks each tool for its actual
output type: an order, symbolic expression, equation array or fitted estimate.
Small independent references can test the transitions. For discovery they
check order/edge conventions and unresolved alternatives. For identification
they check graph-query expression and failure semantics. For estimation they
check the target measure, nuisance fits, truncation and covariance construction.

Numerical disagreements should be classified by cause before they are ranked.
A different estimand is a semantic mismatch. A failed root solve is a numerical
failure. Nonidentification is a scientific outcome. An unsupported covariance
law is a scope limitation. Timing a successful branch while discarding the
others rewards a system for silently avoiding difficult requests. The full
comparison must retain them and distinguish source inspection from executed
behavior. These distinctions make the software survey useful for design and
investment even when it concludes that a component should be deferred.

\chapter{Keeping causal uncertainty through the calculation}
\label{v131:graph-uncertainty}

\section{A graph representation carries a scientific commitment}

A funding analyst may represent the offer rate, customer response and retained
balance by three columns in a matrix. The columns are measurements; the graph
and structural equations give those measurements causal meaning. An adapter
must preserve both. A correctly sized matrix can still encode every arrow in
the wrong direction, and a software object called a mixed graph can still
contain a directed cycle that is inadmissible for the requested identification
algorithm. These errors arise before questions of estimation accuracy.

The inspected LiNGAM base class stores a coefficient in
$B_{\text{target},\text{predictor}}$. It fits each variable against eligible
variables earlier in its selected causal order, optionally removing predictors
excluded by the prior-knowledge matrix. The adaptive-Lasso branch and ordinary
regression branch therefore share an orientation convention. A conversion to
an edge list must interpret a nonzero $B_{jk}$ as $k\to j$.
\cite{v131_sw_lingam}

For a stipulated banking example, let $F$ denote a funding change, $A$ an offer
adjustment and $Y$ the balance response, in declared normalized units:
\[
 A=0.4F+\varepsilon_A,\qquad
 Y=0.1F+2A+\varepsilon_Y.
\]
Holding the disturbance law fixed, a one-unit intervention on $F$ changes $A$
by $0.4$ and $Y$ by $0.1+2(0.4)=0.9$. The latter consists of the direct path
and the mediated path. Transposing this coefficient matrix produces a different
acyclic graph with no path from $F$ to $Y$; its corresponding total effect is
zero. Shape checks and acyclicity checks both pass. An asymmetric intervention
example, rather than a symmetric matrix fixture, detects the semantic error.
The arithmetic is an original project example, not a fit to a bank dataset.
\cite{v131_project_semantics}

LiNGAM's inspected \texttt{estimate\_total\_effect} method regresses the target
on the source and the source's estimated parents. If the requested target is
earlier than the source in the selected causal order, the method warns and
continues. The numerical coefficient remains an output; the warning records a
reason its causal interpretation may be inappropriate. A service that records
only the returned floating-point number would lose that distinction. It should
carry the order, adjustment variables, warning and fitted graph together, and
state whether the request falls within the admitted functional model.
\cite{v131_sw_lingam}

An alternative based on a CPDAG or PAG has different obligations. Its uncertain
arrowheads cannot be collapsed to LiNGAM's selected directed order solely to
make a common schema convenient. An output union or equivalence-class type is
necessary when the method retains several causal possibilities. The common
operation contract should make the statistical and scientific scope visible
without suggesting that one representation is intrinsically superior.

\section{Recursive identification and the reasons for refusal}

y0's inspected ID implementation first handles the absence of interventions,
restricts to outcome ancestors, adds irrelevant variables to the intervention
set and decomposes the graph remaining after treatment removal into districts.
Districts represent connected components of the graph's bidirected component.
The implementation multiplies and marginalizes expressions across the relevant
recursive subproblems. In the connected-district failure branch it raises
\texttt{Unidentifiable}; separate invariant failures raise \texttt{RuntimeError}.
These paths support different service responses. \cite{v131_sw_y0}

For a mixed graph with $A\to Y$ and a latent common cause represented by
$A\leftrightarrow Y$, observational data alone generally cannot distinguish
the intervention response from the common-cause association. The absence of an
identifying functional is a scientific conclusion within that model class.
It is distinct from a malformed graph, an unsupported query or a failed
computation. Treating all four as the same missing value would conceal whether
the analyst needs another measurement, another algorithm or a software repair.

The inspected IDC routine examines whether a conditioning variable can be
exchanged for an intervention using a rule-2 condition. Its helper removes
incoming edges to existing interventions and outgoing edges from the candidate
variable, then delegates a separation test. If the exchange is allowed, IDC
recurses; otherwise it identifies the unconditioned joint query and normalizes
the resulting expression. This establishes the inspected control flow. The
separation routine, expression normalization and all graph-mutilation behavior
require their own correctness evidence. Section~\ref{exec18:pyid-packages}
provides a separation counterexample and excludes this selected native
conditional route pending repair. The control flow described here does not
supersede that restriction. A claim about the whole algorithm cannot be based
solely on recognizing the names of its steps.
\cite{v131_sw_y0}

Graph construction deserves explicit validation at the library boundary.
y0's inspected constructor sets graph metadata, while directed-edge insertion
adds edges and corresponding nodes to both graph components. These methods do
not themselves enforce acyclicity. The identification wrapper should therefore
validate the admitted graph class, query membership, permissible overlap of
treatment/outcome/conditioning sets and any supplied ordering before invoking
the algorithm. The required checks depend on the query language; counterfactual
variables need more than the rules for ordinary intervention queries.
\cite{v131_sw_y0}

A useful qualification set should contain an adjustment example, a front-door
example, a genuinely nonidentified example and malformed inputs with known
failure types. Variable renaming should change names while preserving the
mathematical expression. Adding an irrelevant measured variable should preserve
the effect after valid marginalization. These are proposed behavioral checks;
they have not been run against the newly acquired source here. A symbolic
expression still needs a numerical estimator and a sampling argument before a
bank can use it to choose an offer.

\section{What an estimating-equation column means}

For contributions $\psi_i(\eta)\in\mathbb R^p$, an estimating-equation method
solves $\sum_i\psi_i(\widehat\eta)=0$. A usual independent-unit sandwich takes
\[
 \widehat A=-\frac1n\sum_i\frac{\partial\psi_i}{\partial\eta^\top},
 \qquad
 \widehat B=\frac1n\sum_i\psi_i\psi_i^\top,
 \qquad

\section{Julia effect estimators and the meaning of a reusable result}
\label{exec21:effects-scope}

A servicing manager asks whether an additional contact is worth its cost for
each risk group. A numerical answer requires more than a treatment-effect
method name. The population average, the average among previously contacted
customers, a conditional contrast and a coefficient from residual regression
can differ even when every conditional model is known. Missing outcomes can
change the averaging population again. A reusable interface must carry this
meaning from the business question through the numerical calculation.

The selected Julia sources offer several distinct building blocks.
CausalELM~0.8.0 supplies g-computation and effect learners; CausalForest~0.1.5
implements tree-based contrasts; TMLE~0.20.5 supplies targeted and one-step
estimation; and CausalTables~1.3.4 represents causal data and interventions in
supplied structural models. Their selected source revisions precede the
7~October~2026 cutoff. Their MIT notices permit substantial reuse subject to
retaining the specified notices, but do not establish dependency clearance or
statistical validity. The following comparison concerns inspected source
paths, not native execution or a tested combination of these packages.
\cite{exec21_effects_causalelm,exec21_effects_causalforest,exec21_effects_tmle,exec21_effects_causaltables}

\subsection{An average effect is a population-specific quantity}
\label{exec21:effects-target}

Let $W$ denote pre-contact risk information, $A\in\{0,1\}$ the contact action,
and $Y(a)$ the monetary outcome under action $a$. Under consistency,
conditional exchangeability and treatment positivity, write
$e(w)=\Pr(A=1\mid W=w)$ and
$\tau(w)=E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\mid W=w\}$. The population average treatment effect is
$E\{\tau(W)\}$; the treated-population effect is
$E\{\tau(W)\mid A=1\}$. A prediction vector containing estimated
$\tau(W_i)$ is useful, but does not by itself provide uncertainty for a
selected subgroup or a policy chosen using that vector.

In the inspected CausalELM g-formula path, ATE, ITT and CATE labels use
counterfactual predictions at all supplied covariate rows; the other branch
uses treated rows. The g-computation wrapper averages the contrast, while the
S-learner retains a contrast vector. The T-learner fits each treatment arm and
subtracts its predictions on the supplied covariates. Thus an ITT label only
has an assignment-effect interpretation when the supplied treatment actually
represents assignment; it cannot convert receipt of contact into randomized
offer assignment. Categorical coding, the action clock and the averaging
population must be explicit inputs. \cite{exec21_effects_causalelm}

The same source's double-machine-learning path forms outcome and treatment
residuals and averages foldwise least-squares coefficients. Its fold
constructor slices contiguous rows. Neither the name nor contiguous slicing
supplies a dependence argument for repeated customer records. Even with
oracle nuisance functions and independent observations, a partially linear
coefficient need not be the population average under heterogeneous effects.
To see the distinction, take
$Y=m_0(W)+A\tau(W)+\varepsilon$ with
$E(\varepsilon\mid A,W)=0$. If $m(W)=E(Y\mid W)$, then
$Y-m(W)=(A-e(W))\tau(W)+\varepsilon$. Consequently the population residual
coefficient is
\begin{equation}
\label{exec21:effects-residual}
 \theta_{\rm res}
 =\frac{E[(A-e(W))(Y-m(W))]}{E[(A-e(W))^2]}
 =\frac{E[e(W)(1-e(W))\tau(W)]}{E[e(W)(1-e(W))]}.
\end{equation}
This is an overlap-weighted average in this model. A constant effect or
additional conditions can make it agree with the ATE; cross-fitting alone
does not do so. This derivation concerns the oracle population target and is
not a claim that a fitted implementation attains it in finite samples.
\cite{exec21_effects_causalelm,exec21_effects_reference}

Return to the stipulated servicing population used for the R forest in
Section~\ref{exec21:grfr-target}: the two risk groups have equal population
mass, effects $(-4,12)$ dollars and treatment propensities $(1/2,1/10)$.
Using the same law makes the target comparison across languages explicit;
it supplies no independent empirical corroboration. Exact enumeration gives
\begin{equation}
\label{exec21:effects-targetexample}
 \tau_{\rm ATE}=4,\qquad
 \tau_{\rm ATT}=-\frac43,\qquad
 \theta_{\rm res}=\frac4{17}.
\end{equation}
At an assumed cost of USD~2 per additional contact, the population margin is
USD~2. Subtracting that cost from the residual coefficient instead gives
$-30/17$ dollars. These quantities answer different questions. A proposed
product should refuse a request to relabel the coefficient as the
population-wide incremental value. A separately evaluated targeted policy
could be more useful, but selecting the profitable subgroup and estimating
its value require their own information and uncertainty contract.
\cite{exec21_effects_reference}

\subsection{Source-level uncertainty checks before adoption}
\label{exec21:effects-uncertainty}

The inspected CausalELM generic null routine samples treatment independently
and uniformly from its distinct observed values, or uniformly over its
observed range for a continuous treatment. This does not preserve the
observed treatment count. It also does not reproduce a nonuniform propensity
law or a cluster-randomized design without additional construction. For four
customers assigned exactly one contact, independent fair binary draws retain
that design with probability $4/16=1/4$ and create an empty treatment or
control arm with probability $2/16=1/8$. This exact calculation identifies an
assignment-law mismatch, rather than estimating a package error rate.
\cite{exec21_effects_causalelm,exec21_effects_reference}

There is also a direct dimensional problem in the selected source. For null
statistics $z_1,\ldots,z_B$ and reported statistic $t$, its scalar
\texttt{stderr} expression is
\begin{equation}
\label{exec21:effects-scale}
 s_{\rm code}=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}(t-z_b)^2}{(B-1)\sqrt B}.
\end{equation}
If $t$ and $z_b$ are monetary effects, this expression has squared monetary
units. Multiplication of all outcomes by a positive constant $c$ multiplies
it by $c^2$, whereas a standard error must scale by $c$. With
$(z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4)=(-1,-1,1,1)$ and $t=2$, the expression is $10/3$.
Changing dollars to cents multiplies it by 10,000 rather than 100. This is a
source-level defect in the expression at the selected revision. It does not
require a Julia run to establish the algebra, and it does not establish the
finite-sample behavior of every other package function.
\cite{exec21_effects_causalelm,exec21_effects_reference}

Taking a square root in one location would not settle the larger inference
question. The sampled null law, the centering, the effect being tested and
the relationship between repeated randomization draws and sampling
uncertainty would still need justification. The inspected interval routine
searches a finite grid with tail comparisons against the same null draws;
that code alone is insufficient to claim a valid general confidence-interval
inversion. The proposed reuse decision is therefore to reject unqualified
reuse of this uncertainty path, while retaining the point-estimation family
as a candidate for a separately justified implementation.
\cite{exec21_effects_causalelm}

CausalForest illustrates a different boundary. Its interface exposes
bootstrap or subsampling choices and separate split and leaf samples under
the honest-tree option. However, its outcome-centering forest is fitted
before these per-tree splits. The inspected prediction paths form
within-leaf treated and control weights and return centered-outcome
contrasts. They return point predictions, rather than a calibrated covariance
object. Honesty of the tree split is consequently not sufficient evidence
that all nuisance fitting is independent of evaluation, nor evidence of
equivalence to the separately reviewed \texttt{grf} implementation. A native
comparison should examine the actual nuisance training rows, treatment
coding, arm support in leaves, random-number state and failure behavior
before considering any shared inference contract.
\cite{exec21_effects_causalforest}

\subsection{Targeted estimation, missingness and influence scales}
\label{exec21:effects-tmle}

TMLE exposes nuisance-model choices, outer resampling and propensity
truncation. The selected noncollaborative default uses no outer resampling;
a requested cross-validation design must be supplied and preserved. The
implementation's \texttt{weighted} constructor default is true although
adjacent prose says false, another reason to record actual resolved
configuration. Truncation prevents numerical division by a very small
estimated probability but cannot create absent treatment support. For an
identified ATE in an independent sampling model, the familiar influence
expression clarifies what an adapter must carry:
\begin{equation}
\label{exec21:effects-influence}
\begin{aligned}
 D_i={}&\frac{A_i}{e(W_i)}\{Y_i-m_1(W_i)\}
       -\frac{1-A_i}{1-e(W_i)}\{Y_i-m_0(W_i)\}\\
       &+m_1(W_i)-m_0(W_i)-\psi .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The relevant source combines outcome-residual and counterfactual-mean
components. It stores the standard deviation of the estimated influence
values together with their number, and passes both to the testing
interface. This scale is not already the standard error of the effect.
Conditional asymptotic inference additionally needs suitable nuisance
remainder control, positivity, moments and a sampling-law argument; the
presence of an influence vector does not prove those conditions.
\cite{exec21_effects_tmle}

For example, influence values $(-3,-1,1,3)$ have sample variance $20/3$.
Under the independent mean calculation, the variance of the average is
$5/3$, since $n=4$. Exporting the influence standard deviation as an effect
standard error would miss the factor $\sqrt n$. Conversely, dividing a
quantity that is already a standard error by $\sqrt n$ again would understate
uncertainty. For joint outputs, the source stacks influence vectors and
computes their covariance. A bridge must preserve the identity and order
of contributing customers; equal vector length is insufficient when
different outcomes select different complete cases. Cluster or calendar
dependence requires an appropriate covariance construction, not a new field
name on the independent calculation. \cite{exec21_effects_tmle,exec21_effects_reference}

The missingness documentation is explicit: rows missing variables needed
for estimation are dropped. Without cross-validation, propensity fitting
may use additional records with observed treatment and confounders even
when outcomes are missing. The source's final fluctuation dataset nevertheless
uses complete relevant records. This is useful data reuse, but is not a

\section{Julia effect estimators and the meaning of a reusable result}
\label{exec21:effects-scope}

A servicing manager asks whether an additional contact is worth its cost for
each risk group. A numerical answer requires more than a treatment-effect
method name. The population average, the average among previously contacted
customers, a conditional contrast and a coefficient from residual regression
can differ even when every conditional model is known. Missing outcomes can
change the averaging population again. A reusable interface must carry this
meaning from the business question through the numerical calculation.

The selected Julia sources offer several distinct building blocks.
CausalELM~0.8.0 supplies g-computation and effect learners; CausalForest~0.1.5
implements tree-based contrasts; TMLE~0.20.5 supplies targeted and one-step
estimation; and CausalTables~1.3.4 represents causal data and interventions in
supplied structural models. Their selected source revisions precede the
7~October~2026 cutoff. Their MIT notices permit substantial reuse subject to
retaining the specified notices, but do not establish dependency clearance or
statistical validity. The following comparison concerns inspected source
paths, not native execution or a tested combination of these packages.
\citep{exec21_effects_causalelm,exec21_effects_causalforest,exec21_effects_tmle,exec21_effects_causaltables}

\subsection{An average effect is a population-specific quantity}
\label{exec21:effects-target}

Let $W$ denote pre-contact risk information, $A\in\{0,1\}$ the contact action,
and $Y(a)$ the monetary outcome under action $a$. Under consistency,
conditional exchangeability and treatment positivity, write
$e(w)=\Pr(A=1\mid W=w)$ and
$\tau(w)=E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\mid W=w\}$. The population average treatment effect is
$E\{\tau(W)\}$; the treated-population effect is
$E\{\tau(W)\mid A=1\}$. A prediction vector containing estimated
$\tau(W_i)$ is useful, but does not by itself provide uncertainty for a
selected subgroup or a policy chosen using that vector.

In the inspected CausalELM g-formula path, ATE, ITT and CATE labels use
counterfactual predictions at all supplied covariate rows; the other branch
uses treated rows. The g-computation wrapper averages the contrast, while the
S-learner retains a contrast vector. The T-learner fits each treatment arm and
subtracts its predictions on the supplied covariates. Thus an ITT label only
has an assignment-effect interpretation when the supplied treatment actually
represents assignment; it cannot convert receipt of contact into randomized
offer assignment. Categorical coding, the action clock and the averaging
population must be explicit inputs. \citep{exec21_effects_causalelm}

The same source's double-machine-learning path forms outcome and treatment
residuals and averages foldwise least-squares coefficients. Its fold
constructor slices contiguous rows. Neither the name nor contiguous slicing
supplies a dependence argument for repeated customer records. Even with
oracle nuisance functions and independent observations, a partially linear
coefficient need not be the population average under heterogeneous effects.
To see the distinction, take
$Y=m_0(W)+A\tau(W)+\varepsilon$ with
$E(\varepsilon\mid A,W)=0$. If $m(W)=E(Y\mid W)$, then
$Y-m(W)=(A-e(W))\tau(W)+\varepsilon$. Consequently the population residual
coefficient is
\begin{equation}
\label{exec21:effects-residual}
 \theta_{\rm res}
 =\frac{E[(A-e(W))(Y-m(W))]}{E[(A-e(W))^2]}
 =\frac{E[e(W)(1-e(W))\tau(W)]}{E[e(W)(1-e(W))]}.
\end{equation}
This is an overlap-weighted average in this model. A constant effect or
additional conditions can make it agree with the ATE; cross-fitting alone
does not do so. This derivation concerns the oracle population target and is
not a claim that a fitted implementation attains it in finite samples.
\citep{exec21_effects_causalelm,exec21_effects_reference}

Return to the stipulated servicing population used for the R forest in
Section~\ref{exec21:grfr-target}: the two risk groups have equal population
mass, effects $(-4,12)$ dollars and treatment propensities $(1/2,1/10)$.
Using the same law makes the target comparison across languages explicit;
it supplies no independent empirical corroboration. Exact enumeration gives
\begin{equation}
\label{exec21:effects-targetexample}
 \tau_{\rm ATE}=4,\qquad
 \tau_{\rm ATT}=-\frac43,\qquad
 \theta_{\rm res}=\frac4{17}.
\end{equation}
At an assumed cost of USD~2 per additional contact, the population margin is
USD~2. Subtracting that cost from the residual coefficient instead gives
$-30/17$ dollars. These quantities answer different questions. A proposed
product should refuse a request to relabel the coefficient as the
population-wide incremental value. A separately evaluated targeted policy
could be more useful, but selecting the profitable subgroup and estimating
its value require their own information and uncertainty contract.
\citep{exec21_effects_reference}

and uniformly from its distinct observed values, or uniformly over its

observed treatment count. It also does not reproduce a nonuniform propensity
law or a cluster-randomized design without additional construction. For four
customers assigned exactly one contact, independent fair binary draws retain
that design with probability $4/16=1/4$ and create an empty treatment or
control arm with probability $2/16=1/8$. This exact calculation identifies an
assignment-law mismatch, rather than estimating a package error rate.

statistics $z_1,\ldots,z_B$ and reported statistic $t$, its scalar

\chapter{Design-based estimation, weak information and diagnostics}
\label{sw:design}

The preceding comparisons establish why a common interface must preserve
design-specific meanings. This chapter gathers their consequences for the
analyst's report: state the instrument claim, retain the complete uncertainty
set, distinguish threshold designs and show what a sensitivity parameter does
and does not reveal. The detailed implementation findings remain in the
preceding chapter; the purpose here is to connect them to the bank's decision.

\section{An instrument is a scientific claim}

Suppose a bank uses a rule-based funding incentive \(Z\) as an instrument for
an offered rate \(A\), with retained balances \(Y\) as the outcome and baseline
controls \(W\). Software can encode a regression system, but it cannot establish
that the incentive has no direct effect on balances or that its assignment is
independent of omitted balance determinants. Those are properties of the
economic setting and information process. The package comparison begins after
the instrument, target population, timing and exclusion claim have been stated.

The selected \texttt{ivreg} documentation describes ordinary two-stage least
squares and robust M/MM regression choices. Exogenous regressors in the outcome
equation must also appear among the instruments. An adapter should therefore
retain explicit endogenous, exogenous and instrument column roles rather than
constructing the formula from a single list of predictors. The robust regression
option is an estimator choice; it does not supply a weak-instrument confidence
guarantee. The inspected package is ivreg 0.6-8. The separate AER implementation
is compared in Section~\ref{exec22:riv-inference}; shared function names do not
make the engines interchangeable. That bounded review does not qualify the
whole AER family. \cite{v12_sw_ivreg}

Weak information changes the result contract. The inspected \texttt{ivmodel}
documentation exposes Anderson--Rubin and conditional-likelihood-ratio routines
whose confidence-set outputs are matrices of interval components. A client
that extracts one lower and one upper endpoint can lose disconnectedness or
unboundedness. The appropriate object is
\[
 C=\bigcup_{j=1}^{J} I_j,
\]
where each component \(I_j\) retains its endpoints, possible infinite bounds and
method-specific interpretation. The number of components is part of the result,
not formatting metadata. \cite{v12_sw_ivmodel}

For illustration, a hypothetical reported set
\(C=(-\infty,-2]\cup[3,\infty)\) excludes zero while remaining unbounded in both
directions. Its interval hull is the whole real line. Replacing the set with
that hull changes the question ``is zero in the set?'' and replacing it with a
midpoint invents a finite estimate. Conversely, an empty inversion result is
not equivalent to a missing calculation. The proposed result schema must
preserve these distinctions before any banking decision rule uses the output.
This hypothetical set is not a computed result from ivmodel.

The two R packages are therefore complementary candidates. ivreg supplies a
regression interface with specific estimation and diagnostic choices; ivmodel
supplies selected weak-information test/inversion interfaces. A matched trial
must align instruments, controls, scaling, sampling assumptions and covariance
choices. It must retain weak and zero first stages, singular designs and
unbounded sets. A regression returning quickly on a well-conditioned example
would not qualify the weak-information case, and the presence of an inversion
API would not establish coverage for dependent bank panels.
The source-level CLR failure substitution described in
Section~\ref{exec22:riv-inference} also remains a condition on reuse:
a numerical failure must not be reported as scientific rejection merely
because the returned p-value is zero.

\section{Regression discontinuity is a family of designs}

A credit policy can change at a score cutoff, but several causal questions can
be attached to that threshold. A sharp design studies a deterministic assignment
change. A fuzzy design uses a discontinuity in treatment probability. A kink
design studies a change in slope. These require different estimands and
denominators. Treating them as one generic local regression would make an
apparently comparable benchmark compare different scientific problems.

The inspected rdrobust 4.0.0 documentation exposes sharp, fuzzy and kink
settings, local-polynomial choices, bias correction, bandwidth choices and
variance options. The adapter should bind the cutoff and running-variable
units to the result and export the actual bandwidth and inference settings.
The bandwidth for a point-estimation objective and the choices underlying a
bias-corrected interval cannot be silently conflated. The saved 4.0.0 snapshot
predates the literature cutoff. Section~\ref{exec22:riv-scope} explains why
the subsequently authenticated CRAN publication time retains that distribution
for the client cutoff; it does not settle every upstream channel's history.
\cite{v12_sw_rdrobust}

For a fuzzy design, the treatment jump matters as much as the outcome jump.
If a local effect is expressed schematically as \(\tau_Y/\tau_A\), a small
\(\tau_A\) produces an unstable ratio even when each fitted regression has a
clean numerical convergence report. The bank's first question should be
whether the score rule changes the specified treatment in the relevant
population. The software trial should vary that first-stage jump and preserve
weak cases rather than selecting only a strong demonstration.

rddensity supplies a different operation: local-polynomial density or
manipulation diagnostics near the cutoff. Such diagnostics can challenge a
design, but failure to reject a discontinuity does not verify the assignment
mechanism or continuity of potential outcomes. An interface that displays
``RD valid'' after a density test would convert one diagnostic into a much
stronger scientific statement. A useful report instead gives the test,
bandwidth, support and interpretation limit alongside other design evidence.
Discrete scores and mass points require explicit attention. \cite{v12_sw_rddensity}

rdlocrand represents another approach, based on a declared local-randomization
window. Its selected documentation states that a positive polynomial order
uses asymptotic inference and that confidence-set inversion is performed over
a supplied grid. Thus a finite grid endpoint is not automatically a finite
confidence bound. If all evaluated values near the boundary remain accepted,
the result should say that the search is truncated. Extending the grid is a
computational remedy; it is not evidence for the local-randomization assumption.
Window selection, assignment probabilities and the intervention must still be
recorded. \cite{v12_sw_rdlocrand}

These packages should be evaluated as a collection of design-specific
operations. The proposed integration uses a common report for the score,
cutoff, assignment rule and target, then separate method records. The product
should not expose a single switch called ``robust RD'' that hides whether the
calculation is continuity-based local-polynomial inference or local-randomization
inference. The alternatives may both be useful, but they answer their questions
under different assumptions.

\section{Sensitivity parameters are not missing truth}

Two other R interfaces provide useful sensitivity summaries. sensemakr
parameterizes omitted-variable sensitivity through partial \(R^2\) quantities
and observed-covariate benchmarks. A large benchmark asks how conclusions would
change if an omitted variable had specified residual associations; it does not
measure the actual association of an unobserved variable. The bank must identify
what makes a proposed benchmark plausible, and the report should retain both
the chosen benchmark and the effect scale. \cite{v12_sw_sensemakr}

The selected EValue \texttt{evalues.RR} interface takes a risk ratio and optional
confidence limits and reports E-values for the point and the near-null confidence
limit. This is a particular scale-specific sensitivity operation. A default
probability difference, a standardized regression coefficient and a net present
value should not be passed to it as if they were risk ratios. Any conversion
needs an explicit target and assumptions. An E-value does not estimate a
confounding correction or certify an absence of confounding. \cite{v12_sw_evalue}

These tools can make a funding or credit recommendation more intelligible:
they expose how much an assumption would need to change before a conclusion
changes. They cannot supply verified instrument exclusion, known ownership,
correct record inclusion or a gold audit label. Their adoption is therefore
conditional on a result contract that separates observed data summaries,
user-supplied sensitivity assumptions and causal conclusions.

change. A fuzzy design uses a discontinuity in treatment probability. A kink
design studies a change in slope. These require different estimands and
denominators. Treating them as one generic local regression would make an
apparently comparable benchmark compare different scientific problems.

correct record inclusion or a gold audit label. Their adoption is therefore
conditional on a result contract that separates observed data summaries,
user-supplied sensitivity assumptions and causal conclusions.

\chapter{Longitudinal regimes, heterogeneous effects and continuous doses}
\label{v13:sw-regimes}

The detailed comparisons distinguish complete policy evaluation from components
that estimate heterogeneity or a dose curve. This chapter brings those choices
back to a small set of servicing and incentive requests. Its finite examples
show why the same data field or output name cannot determine which component
the bank needs. The preceding source studies supply the implementation limits;
the task here is to preserve them when composing the workflow.

\section{A sequence of decisions changes the software contract}

Servicing involves repeated decisions. A customer may receive a reminder, a
repayment plan and later a restructuring offer, with delinquency and contact
history changing between actions. An operation for a single binary treatment
does not become a longitudinal estimator by adding a time column. The target
must state which histories the policy observes, when actions occur, what ends
follow-up and how default or account closure changes the outcome.

Let $L_t$ be information available before action $A_t$, and let
$H_t=(\bar L_t,\bar A_{t-1})$ denote the observed history. A deterministic regime
$d$ supplies $A_t=d_t(H_t)$. For a terminal outcome $Y$, its value is
$V(d)=\mathbb E(Y^d)$. Under the required consistency, sequential
exchangeability and positivity conditions, a g-computation construction can
integrate an outcome regression against the covariate transition laws induced
by the intervention. Schematically,
\[
 V(d)=\int m(\bar l_T,\bar d_T)
             \prod_{t=0}^{T}p(l_t\mid\bar l_{t-1},\bar d_{t-1})
             \,d\bar l_T.
\]
The notation suppresses censoring and competing events, which must be specified
in an actual application. The product follows the intervention history; it is
not the factual joint distribution with treatment columns overwritten afterward.

The software comparison should therefore examine covariate transitions,
intervention callbacks, history updates, horizon conventions, simulation error
and sampling uncertainty. It should also compare parametric g-computation with
weighting and longitudinal targeted estimation on the same policy and population.
Disagreement over a default horizon or competing event can dominate any
difference in optimization speed.

\section{pygformula exposes the history and event choices}

The inspected \texttt{ParametricGformula} class accepts individual and time
identifiers, time-varying covariate names/types/models, custom histories, custom
fit/prediction functions and intervention descriptions. Its outcome options
include survival, continuous end-of-follow-up and binary end-of-follow-up.
Separate arguments address competing events, whether to treat them as censoring,
and a censoring model used for natural-course comparisons. \cite{v13_sw_pygformula}

If default prevents later repayment, a default-free survival probability and a
cumulative incidence of repayment are different targets. If closing an account
merely hides future payment information, a censoring argument is needed. Asking
software to treat a competing event as censoring changes the scientific
experiment; the decision requires substantive justification and must survive
the library, CLI and agent interfaces.

The class documentation sets the number of bootstrap samples to zero by
default. The selected fit path invokes separate bootstrap work when samples
are requested. Thus the presence of bootstrap support does not imply that a
particular invocation produced sampling intervals. The helper review in
Section~\ref{sec:exec24-longitudinal-python} establishes whole-subject history
resampling and documents the failed-replicate handling discrepancy. That source
finding does not qualify arbitrary calendar dependence or the fitted intervals.
The adapter must retain the actual sampling unit and complete failure counts.
\cite{v13_sw_pygformula}

on fitted transition laws, additional simulated trajectories reduce numerical
integration error. They do not provide new bank observations or reduce the

and availability clocks, action timing, history definitions, horizon, competing
events and intervention semantics. It records whether uncertainty was requested
and actually obtained. Natural-course reproduction is a diagnostic: matching
factual outcomes does not prove that intervention predictions are valid.

should remain explicit, even if simulation can generate a numeric outcome.

complete simulation and bootstrap paths, environment and dependency terms, and
matched comparisons with R implementations and other longitudinal estimators.
The retained source studies resolve selected simulation and bootstrap questions;
they do not replace those native qualification requirements.

been learned. Policy selection and its evaluation are additional operations.

\section{grf: binary heterogeneity and continuous slopes are different targets}

The inspected \texttt{causal\_forest} documentation defines a binary-treatment
conditional effect and, for continuous treatment, describes the conditional
covariance ratio
\[
 \tau(x)=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,A\mid X=x)}
                    {\operatorname{Var}(A\mid X=x)}.
\]
The interface accepts nuisance predictions, clusters and equal cluster
weighting, honesty, subsampling, tuning, grouped trees for uncertainty and a
seed for its native random-number generator. Defaults include 2,000 trees,
honesty enabled and no tuning. These options define a specific statistical and
computational operation; they are not optional metadata for a reproducible
comparison. \cite{v13_sw_grf}

For binary treatment, an effect conditional on $X=x$ differs from a population
average unless it is integrated over the desired population. For continuous
treatment, a slope-like summary differs from a finite contrast
$\mu(a_1,x)-\mu(a_0,x)$. Calling both outputs ``uplift'' obscures the decision.
A bank deciding whether to increase an incentive from one specified amount to
another needs the latter contrast, or a justified approximation to it.

An exact project example makes the discrepancy visible. Suppose the stipulated
mean outcome, in CNY, is
\[
 \mu(a)=20a-3a^2,\qquad A\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,2].
\]
This is a synthetic response curve, not a fitted bank relationship. Its
covariance slope is
\[

\]
The finite change from dose one to dose two is instead
\[
 \mu(2)-\mu(1)=28-17=11.
\]

difference is a target difference, not a forest error. Multiplying the slope
by a unit change would overstate this stipulated finite benefit by three CNY.

outcome definition. \cite{v13_project_exact}

each branch equal total weight is different from giving each customer equal
weight when branch sizes differ. The chosen measure affects both the target
and the interpretation of heterogeneity. An adapter should require an explicit
population-weight policy and record the effective cluster structure; it should
not silently translate a customer population into an equal-branch population.

The R wrapper's seed, threading and native interface make an R/native adapter
a natural candidate. This inspection does not qualify the C++ training,
prediction or variance implementation. The observed repository GPL text also
requires a complete licensing and distribution review before a port or embedded
binary decision. A rewrite is not automatically preferable to a well-specified
boundary around the original implementation. \cite{v13_sw_grf}

\section{A generalized propensity score is a density component}

CausalGPS's inspected \texttt{estimate\_gps} function accepts continuous
exposure and covariates, a formula, normal or kernel density mode and a
SuperLearner library selection. In its normal branch, the fitted exposure mean
and a residual standard deviation enter a normal density. Its kernel branch
fits exposure and residual scaling and calls a separate density helper. Returned
fields include identity, exposure, generalized propensity score, fitted mean
and scale, and residuals. \cite{v13_sw_causalgps}

For continuous $A$, a generalized propensity score is a conditional density
$r(a,x)=f_{A\mid X}(a\mid x)$, not a probability in $[0,1]$. Its units depend

\[
 f_{B\mid X}(b\mid x)=\frac1c f_{A\mid X}(b/c\mid x).
\]
Thus converting an incentive from CNY to hundreds of CNY changes the density
numerically. A bridge that normalizes every ``propensity'' into a binary
probability can corrupt continuous-treatment calculations. Exposure units and
the exact density evaluation points belong in the contract.

The observed-density function alone does not provide a dose-response estimator.
To compare feasible doses one needs densities or another identified construction
at the relevant counterfactual doses, an outcome model or weighting/matching
procedure, support diagnostics and an uncertainty argument.
Section~\ref{sec:exec24-dose-response-reuse} follows the density delegate,
transformation factors and downstream weighting. It identifies the selected
kernel branch's residual-density export and the conditions needed for an
original-scale density interpretation. Those restrictions must survive any
cross-package conversion. The retained source analysis establishes a component
and concrete qualification cases; it does not establish the complete causal
workflow.

A useful banking support diagnostic asks whether both proposed incentive levels
occur with adequate conditional support among the intended customers. The
normal model can assign positive density far beyond observed incentive choices;
mathematical positivity of a parametric density is not evidence of practical
overlap. Reporting density values together with observed range, local support
and model sensitivity is more informative than presenting a successful fit as
permission to extrapolate. The observed package declaration is GPL-3; complete
dependency and redistribution choices remain part of adoption review.

\section{causaldrf describes a full response surface, with different limits}

The inspected \texttt{hi\_est} documentation describes fitting a treatment
model, a GPS-adjusted outcome response surface, and predictions averaged over
customers at requested dose-grid values. It lists Normal, LogNormal, transformed
normal, Poisson, negative-binomial, Gamma and Binomial treatment models, and
returns fitted model and parameter records. This supports a documented
response-surface comparison; it is not an execution result or a review of every
internal estimator~\citep{v13_sw_causaldrf}.

Writing a fitted response surface as $\widehat m(a,r)$, the described averaging
operation is of the form
\[
 \widehat\mu(a)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
                      \widehat m\{a,\widehat r(a,X_i)\}.
\]
The GPS is evaluated at the proposed dose for each customer, rather than simply
reusing every customer's density at their observed dose. A finite effect then
requires a specified comparator, $\widehat\mu(a_1)-\widehat\mu(a_0)$.
A curve ordinate is an expected outcome, and labeling it as an effect without
the comparator misstates the answer.

constraint permits only three incentive levels, interpolation at arbitrary
levels has no immediate operating interpretation. If the optimum is selected
from a dense grid using the same fitted surface, uncertainty in that selection

should therefore distinguish fixed contrasts, whole curves and policy
optimization, and explain which one is actually supported.

The observed DESCRIPTION declares MIT plus a separate LICENSE file. The
initial documentation review did not include that accompanying notice or a
complete implementation review~\citep{v13_sw_causaldrf}. The later source
review recovered and inspected the notice, identifying the year and copyright
holder~\citep{v131_sw_causaldrf}. The appropriate decision remains a provisional
reference or adapter candidate: full implementation, interval behavior and
transitive dependency terms still require qualification. A recovered notice
is not a complete dependency inventory, and documented point estimation is
not evidence of qualified confidence intervals.

\section{A common servicing and incentive benchmark}

These components should be compared through a small set of declared banking
queries. One query fixes a two-period servicing regime and a terminal repayment
outcome. Another fixes a binary offer and asks for heterogeneity. A third fixes
two continuous incentive levels and asks for their net financial difference.
Each query has its own sampling unit, support requirements, feasible actions
and reference functional. A tool may be appropriate for one and unsupported
for another; that is useful information for architecture.

The comparison should retain a model that fits factual outcomes but fails an
intervention assumption, a weak-support population, a changed event definition
and a changed treatment unit. It should separately measure statistical error,
simulation error, numerical failure and computation. For longitudinal work,
the complete cost includes fitting transitions and histories, simulating
interventions, obtaining uncertainty and reporting diagnostics. Timing one
prediction call omits most of the workflow the bank would operate.

An eventual selection can combine components: symbolic identification, a
longitudinal engine, a heterogeneous-effect estimator and a dose-response
component can coexist behind one semantic contract. The common contract must
preserve their distinct assumptions and outputs. It should make unsupported
requests explicit rather than coercing every query into the nearest available
estimator.

\chapter{Longitudinal treatment, monitoring and mediation}
\label{sw:longitudinal}

Policy choice also determines what the bank observes. Monitoring can change
record availability, and a recorded engagement measure may become a mediator
rather than a baseline control. The compact example here connects these roles
to the detailed longitudinal and mediation comparisons, so that an interface
preserves the question before routing it to an R estimator.

\section{The history is part of the intervention}

The servicing problem is naturally sequential. An initial action \(A_0\), such
as an early contact, can change a later financial condition \(L_1\). A second
action \(A_1\) is then chosen using that condition, and a later account cost
\(Y\) is observed. The variable \(L_1\) can be both a consequence of the first
action and a determinant of the second. Treating it as an ordinary baseline
control erases that temporal structure. Treating both actions as one binary
indicator can erase the policy being evaluated.

Consider a finite project mechanism in which \(A_0,L_1,A_1\) are binary and
\[
 \Pr(L_1=1\mid\operatorname{do}(A_0=0))=0.8,
 \qquad
 \Pr(L_1=1\mid\operatorname{do}(A_0=1))=0.4.
\]
Conditional mean cost, in CNY per account over a fixed horizon, is specified as
\[
 m(a_0,l,a_1)=100l-50a_1l+20a_0+10a_1.
\]
The initial action costs 20 and reduces the chance of the adverse condition.
The later action costs 10 and reduces adverse-condition cost by 50 when that
condition is present. These numbers define the example; they are not estimates
of actual bank effects.

For a second-stage rule \(d\), replacing the two action equations gives
\begin{equation}
 V(a_0,d)=\sum_{l=0}^{1}m(a_0,l,d(l))
             \Pr(L_1=l\mid\operatorname{do}(A_0=a_0)).
 \label{sw:finite-policy}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{sw:finite-policy} follows by enumerating the two possible
conditions under the specified intervention. It yields
\[
 V(0,0)=80,\qquad V(1,l\mapsto l)=44,\qquad V(1,1)=50.
\]
The adaptive policy is better than always giving the later action because it
avoids paying for that action in accounts without the adverse condition.
No policy-learning or global-optimality theorem is needed for this comparison
of three explicitly specified rules. A proposed general optimizer would have
additional obligations.

Now hold \(A_0=0\) and consider an observed logger that gives \(A_1=1\) with
probability 0.9 when \(L_1=1\), and 0.1 otherwise. The observed treated group
contains a disproportionate share of accounts with the adverse condition.
Direct enumeration gives
\[
 E[Y\mid A_1=1,A_0=0]=58.64865\ldots,
 \qquad E[Y\mid A_1=0,A_0=0]=30.76923\ldots.
\]
The observational difference is approximately \(+27.88\). Yet the intervention
contrast that treats everyone at the second stage, at \(A_0=0\), is
\(V(0,1)-V(0,0)=50-80=-30\). The sign reversal is selection by an observed
time-varying condition in this mechanism. It shows why an interface must retain
the treatment history and the distribution over which the policy is valued.

In an application, evaluating an expression like
\eqref{sw:finite-policy} from observations requires substantive assumptions
connecting observed conditional distributions to the intervention model. It
also requires that relevant histories and actions have support. The example
supplies its structural law directly; it does not demonstrate that a bank's
logger, monitoring or missingness mechanisms satisfy those assumptions.

\section{Point treatment and sequential software have different contracts}

The selected tmle interface concerns binary point-treatment effects with
missingness and subject-ID options. It is a candidate for a suitable static
effect question; that does not make it an arbitrary longitudinal policy engine.
The versioned documentation also contains a treatment-missingness wording
difference between DESCRIPTION and the selected Delta argument.
Section~\ref{exec20:rfx-scope} resolves the selected implementation's contract:
missing treatment and baseline covariates are rejected, while the no-variation
route estimates an outcome mean. Section~\ref{sec:exec24-tmle-reuse} retains
the additional interval and resampling restrictions. A convenient argument
name cannot extend those admitted meanings. \cite{v12_sw_tmle}

stremr's selected sequential g-computation and TMLE documentation is closer to
the servicing problem. It accepts time points, sequential outcome-model
formulas, treatment intervention probabilities, monitoring intervention
probabilities and related weighting choices. Treatment and monitoring are
separate intervention components. A bank that increases contact may also
increase the chance that financial stress is recorded; holding monitoring
fixed and changing it are different policy questions. The interface should
name which of these is being evaluated. \cite{v12_sw_stremr}

while the source review in Section~\ref{sec:exec23-longr-workers} finds a
corresponding branch. That discrepancy remains a qualification question;
it is not evidence of failure in every native call. The proposed profile
withholds that option pending qualification. Weight truncation and stabilization
are choices, and the reviewed stopping loops can differ from the requested
cap. A wrapper should report the effective weights, actual updates, final
residuals and warnings after execution. A truncated weight or stopped numerical
iteration is not evidence that positivity or statistical accuracy has been
established. It is part of the approximation and diagnostic record.

survtmle addresses another closely related but distinct problem: right
censoring, competing failures and cumulative incidence. Its selected interface
supports two treatment values. A competing failure must not be recoded as
ordinary censoring simply to fit a common input schema. In a banking setting,
default, repayment, restructuring and account closure can correspond to
different outcome or observation events, depending on the question. The
adapter must preserve the cause, horizon and target, and the analyst must
justify their interpretation. \cite{v12_sw_survtmle}

TMLE, sequential g-computation/TMLE, and competing-risk cumulative incidence.

should not imply scientific substitutability. The proposed tests include
treatment-confounder feedback, monitoring-dependent recording, administrative
censoring, absent action support, and the distinction between a failure event
and a missing observation. These trials must assess the specific estimand and
sampling law; a successful fit on complete independent records does not
qualify a dynamic bank panel.

The age of a saved distribution is recorded as evidence about that distribution,
not as a verdict on project maintenance. In particular, older stremr and
survtmle snapshots do not prove abandonment. Conversely, a recent version
string does not demonstrate correctness of every documented feature. Build
compatibility and method validity require their own observations.
